title: Molecular self-assembly prints the capacitor lattice instead of EUV
idea: Scale shift from scanner optics down to molecular length: a high-chi block copolymer (PS-b-PDMS or PS-b-PMMA) self-assembles into a hexagonal cylinder lattice that matches the honeycomb capacitor array, registered by an ArF-immersion guide pattern at 4x pitch; sequential infiltration synthesis turns one block into an alumina hardmask for the hole etch.
why: Removes 1-2 EUV exposures (capacitor hole, landing pad) from Fact 4; ~15-25% lower array litho cost per wafer because the molecule, not the scanner, sets the pitch.

title: Panel-scale nanoimprinted oxide gain cells on depreciated display lines
idea: Jump from a 0.07 m2 wafer to 5.5 m2 Gen-8.5 display mother-glass: retired LCD/OLED lines run panel-scale nanoimprint at ~50 nm half-pitch to build 8 stacked low-temperature oxide-semiconductor 2T0C gain-cell tiers, which are diced into memory tiles and bonded to silicon periphery chiplets.
why: Capital intensity: display fabs are fully depreciated and processed area costs ~50-100x less per m2 than a DRAM wafer, so ~8 tiers at 50 nm can reach cost-per-bit parity for a capacity tier without new fab capex.

title: Wafer-scale memory plate: one undiced wafer per rack sled
idea: Shift the product unit from die up to whole wafer: stitched identical array fields with redundant inter-field links, no dicing, no per-die packaging; the 300 mm wafer is mounted on a cooled sled board with edge connectors as a ~1-2 TB rack memory plate that routes around dead fields at boot.
why: Deletes dicing, packaging and per-die known-good-die test (~15-25% of finished DRAM cost) plus ~5% scribe area; I/O periphery is shared across fields.

title: Rack-level remapping lets fabs ship dies without laser repair
idea: Move repair up from the die (fuse banks, spare rows, laser repair station) to the rack: each die ships with an OTP defect map and the CXL memory-pool controller remaps around bad 1 MB regions in its page tables, accepting dies with up to ~3% dead capacity.
why: Eliminates laser-repair tools and most redundancy area (~3-5% of die), shortens test, and lifts effective yield 10-20 points on a new node (Facts 4, 7).

title: Trade lithography node for tier count: ArF-only 3D DRAM
idea: Shift density from the litho-bound x-y plane to the deposition-bound z axis: a horizontal-capacitor 3D DRAM drawn at F~38 nm with ArF single exposures only, reaching bit-density parity at ~120-150 Si/SiGe epitaxial tiers patterned by one high-AR slit plus staircase per block.
why: Zero EUV layers and ~40% fewer masks; deposition/etch passes cost ~5x less per wafer than EUV exposures, so capex per bit falls even with many tiers (Facts 2, 4).

title: Surface chemistry inherits one mask through four self-aligned layers
idea: Shift patterning from the reticle to the monolayer: after a single bitline exposure, small-molecule inhibitors (aminosilanes on oxide, thiols on metal) bind to only one surface type, so area-selective ALD grows plugs, landing pads and caps exactly on prior features with no new masks.
why: Removes 3-4 masks and their overlay budget per array (~10% fewer litho passes) and cuts edge-placement failures (Fact 4).

title: Grow capacitor pillars bottom-up instead of etching 70:1 holes
idea: Invert the length-scale problem: rather than etching 1.5 um-deep holes, grow vertical Si nanowires from CMOS-compatible catalyst dots (Al or Cu-silicide) placed on the capacitor lattice sites, then wrap them in ZrO2/HfO2 and a top electrode; aspect ratio becomes a function of growth time, not etch physics.
why: Breaks the AR 60-75:1 etch wall (Fact 1): AR ~150:1 for Cs >8 fF without cryogenic etch tools, removing the single costliest etch step.

title: Datacenter fleets as ore: reverse-fab reclaim of retired DRAM dies
idea: Scale shift from fab to fleet: DIMMs retired after 4-6 years are laser/chemically decapped, dies are retested and rebinned, then re-assembled onto new substrates or CXL expander cards as capacity-tier memory with stronger ECC.
why: Adds bits with ~zero fab capex; a hyperscaler fleet could recover 30-60% of retired bits at <20% of new-die cost.

title: Nanoimprint the periodic array, DUV the periphery: mix-and-match
idea: Exploit that a DRAM mat is a perfect crystal: one e-beam master is replicated into imprint templates that stamp the whole array layer (holes or lines) at 12-16 nm half-pitch per field, while ArF scanners pattern only the irregular periphery.
why: Replaces the most expensive EUV array layers; an imprint tool is ~1/5 the cost and ~1/10 the energy of EUV per layer (Fact 4).

title: Maskless wafer-flash interference lattice with a coarse cut mask
idea: Expose the entire wafer's capacitor-hole lattice in one flash with three-beam 193 nm laser interference (hexagonal pattern, no mask, no projection lens), reach final pitch by self-aligned pitch splitting, and erase the lattice outside the arrays with a cheap KrF keep/cut mask.
why: An interference rig is <$5M versus ~$200M EUV, and a wafer-scale flash takes seconds instead of ~100 field exposures (Fact 4).

title: Accept 16 ms retention to delete recessed-channel process steps
idea: Time-shift the refresh interval from 64 ms to 16 ms and let a smart controller absorb the extra refreshes on a capacity-tier product; the looser leakage target lets a shallow-recess planar access transistor replace the buried saddle-fin, deleting the recess etch, halo implants and their masks.
why: Removes ~6-10 process steps and 2-3 implant masks (Facts 3, 4) for ~5-8% lower wafer cost, trading some refresh energy on low-activity memory.

title: 5 mm2 DRAM dielets tolerate dirtier fabs via exponential yield
idea: Shrink the die from ~70 mm2 to ~5 mm2 dielets: under Poisson yield a 3x higher defect density still yields >90%, so the line can run looser particle control and fewer inline inspections; dielets are assembled by die-to-wafer hybrid bonding onto a logic base.
why: Cuts cleanroom-class and inspection capex (~10-15% of a fab) and lifts yield 20-30% on immature lines (Facts 4, 6).

title: Bond eight DRAM wafers before dicing: TSV-free wafer-stacked HBM
idea: Replace die-by-die microbump stacking with sequential wafer-on-wafer hybrid bonding of 8-12 DRAM wafers, using fine-pitch bonded vias through 5 um-thinned silicon instead of large TSVs, then dice the finished stack once.
why: Cuts the HBM TSV area tax (Fact 6) by 2-3x and deletes per-die microbump and underfill steps; throughput scales per wafer, not per die.

title: Shift burn-in from oven hours to fleet weeks
idea: Time-shift the reliability screen: skip factory burn-in ovens and long retention tests, ship dies with on-die BIST that runs adaptive stress patterns during the first weeks of server idle time, and retire weak rows through the host before data is trusted.
why: Burn-in and test are ~10% of DRAM cost and heavy capital; cutting them ~70% saves ~5-7% per bit and frees tester capacity.

title: Four charge levels per cell doubles bits without new tools
idea: Store 2 bits per 1T1C cell as four charge levels, read by a time-to-digital sense amplifier that measures how long the bitline takes to develop rather than its polarity; same fab, same masks, same node.
why: 1.6-1.8x bits per wafer net of larger sense amps with zero new capex (Fact 4); fights the charge wall (Fact 1), hence high risk.

title: Warehouse fab: sealed tool pods replace the ballroom cleanroom
idea: Shrink the controlled environment from building scale (ISO 3-5 ballroom with massive HVAC) to the cubic metre around each wafer: every tool sits in a sealed N2 mini-environment linked by enclosed overhead wafer tubes, so the shell is an ordinary warehouse.
why: Cleanroom construction and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab capex and a large energy load; could save $2-4B on a $15B fab and about a year of build time.

title: Memory futures: decade offtake contracts pre-fund new DRAM fabs
idea: Shift capital timing: hyperscalers buy 10-year capacity futures with upfront pre-delivery payments (as airlines do for aircraft), which collateralize fab construction loans and set a price band.
why: Moves capital intensity off the memory maker's balance sheet; ~30% of fab capex pre-funded lowers the cost of capital by several points.

title: Bond cheap-logic periphery under a minimal-mask array wafer
idea: Split the die across two wafers: the 49% periphery is built on a mature 28 nm logic wafer, the array on a stripped-down ~15-mask array-only wafer, and the two are joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding at sub-1 um pitch.
why: Periphery stops consuming the expensive DRAM process (Fact 7): array density +40-60% and each wafer runs on the tool set where it is cheapest.

title: Nanosecond laser crystallization builds silicon tiers atop finished arrays
idea: Time-shift the thermal budget from furnace hours to nanoseconds: deposit amorphous Si on each finished tier and melt-recrystallize it with a ~30 ns excimer pulse seeded through small vias, so it becomes near-single-crystal while layers below stay under 400 C; repeat per tier for monolithic 3D DRAM.
why: Enables monolithic tier stacking without wafer bonding (Fact 2); each extra tier costs a deposition plus a laser pass, not a new wafer.

title: MicroLED-style mass transfer of 100 um DRAM micro-tiles onto panels
idea: Borrow microLED mass transfer: release 100 um DRAM micro-tiles from the wafer by undercut etch and pick 10,000 at once with elastomer stamps onto large panels carrying RDL and logic chiplets.
why: Panel-scale assembly cuts packaging cost per bit 3-5x and harvests good tiles from every wafer at near-100% (Fact 6).

title: Slow long-bitline capacity die with only two metal layers
idea: Make a second DRAM product with 1024 cells per bitline (vs ~512) and two metal layers, accepting ~50 ns access and using a low-capacitance air-gap bitline to keep sense margin; the higher cell-to-sense-amp ratio halves sense-amp count.
why: Periphery falls from ~49% toward ~30% of the die (Fact 7) and ~4 metal/via masks disappear, ~15% lower cost per bit for capacity memory.

title: Short-loop micro-line compresses yield learning from years to months
idea: Time-shift the learning loop: a dedicated micro-line runs 30-50-step short-loop wafers containing only the module under study with 5-day cycle times, feeding fixes to the main line instead of waiting for 90-day full-flow wafers.
why: Yield ramp is where new fabs burn billions; 4-6x more learning cycles per year shortens ramp by ~12 months.

title: One vacuum cluster runs forty capacitor steps without queuing
idea: Collapse the wafer's timescale: a linear vacuum cluster integrates ~40 sequential deposition, etch and clean steps of the capacitor module, so the wafer never leaves vacuum or waits in a FOUP queue; the module goes from ~20 days to ~1 day of cycle time.
why: Cuts WIP inventory capital and queue-time defects; fewer transfers raise yield and total fab cycle time drops ~25%.

title: Anodized aluminum pores template capacitors from a U.S. wet bench
idea: Swap plasma etch for slow electrochemistry: a film of U.S.-smelted aluminum is anodized for hours in acid and self-organizes into hexagonal pores with >100:1 aspect ratio, guided by a shallow imprinted dimple pattern; the alumina becomes the mold for TiN/high-k/TiN capacitor shells.
why: Replaces the hardest high-AR etch (Fact 1) with bath equipment costing ~1% of a cryo-etch tool, buildable domestically; AR 100-200:1 gives Cs ~8-10 fF.

title: Talbot self-imaging prints the cell lattice with U.S. lasers
idea: Displacement Talbot lithography: a 1:1 periodic phase mask from a U.S. mask shop and a U.S.-built 213/266 nm solid-state laser self-image the lattice across the whole wafer with near-unlimited depth of focus; no projection optics, so no imported scanner.
why: Removes EUV/ArF scanner dependence (single-supplier chokepoint) for array layers (Fact 4) with a ~$3-8M domestic tool.

title: Atom-precise probe master cloned through a template family tree
idea: Time shift: spend weeks writing one perfect master array by parallel scanning-probe hydrogen-depassivation lithography on U.S.-built tools, then clone it through generations of imprint templates (1 -> 100 -> 10,000) so the slow atomic write is amortized over millions of wafers.
why: Sub-10 nm array templates without EUV; master cost falls below ~$0.01 per wafer.

title: Domestic multi-column e-beam writes periphery and cut layers maskless
idea: Use thousands of parallel miniature e-beam columns built in the U.S. to direct-write only the sparse, irregular layers (periphery contacts, cut masks, chip IDs), while self-assembly or imprint handles the dense arrays.
why: Eliminates ~10-15 masks per product ($10-20M per node) and imported scanners on those layers; product variants turn in days.

title: Colorado molybdenum replaces Chinese tungsten from mine to monolayer
idea: Vertical integration across scales: Colorado molybdenite is refined domestically into MoO2Cl2/MoCl5 ALD precursors, and molybdenum replaces tungsten in buried wordlines and contacts, where its shorter electron mean free path gives lower resistance below 20 nm width.
why: Removes the ~80% China tungsten chokepoint; ~20-30% lower wordline resistance permits longer wordlines and less periphery.

title: Kerfless epitaxial wafers: one seed crystal reused fifty times
idea: DRAM uses only the top few microns of a 775 um wafer: grow a 20-50 um epitaxial Si film on a porous-Si release layer atop a reusable seed wafer, lift it off onto a low-cost domestic carrier, and re-polish the seed for ~50 reuses.
why: Cuts Czochralski pulling, quartz crucibles and polysilicon per wafer by ~10-30x; Michigan polysilicon and U.S. epi reactors suffice.

title: Liberty-ship fab modules: identical U.S. fabs built serially
idea: Time-compress fab construction from 3-5 years to ~15 months by freezing one standard 20k-wafer-per-month module (shell, utilities, layout) and building copies serially from prefabricated U.S.-made subfab skids, as WWII yards cut ship build time 10x through repetition.
why: Learning-curve cost ~20-30% lower by the fifth copy; earlier revenue cuts interest during construction (capital intensity).

title: Supercritical CO2 drying lets capacitors stand without support lattices
idea: Scale insight: at the nanoscale, capillary forces from the final rinse topple tall pillars, which is why a nitride support lattice (extra deposition, litho, etch) is needed; drying in supercritical CO2 from domestic industrial gas (zero surface tension) lets freestanding pillars reach ~100:1.
why: Removes 1-2 masks and ~6 support-lattice steps; taller pillars add ~30% Cs (Fact 1).

title: Deep-trench storage revival from America's eDRAM heritage
idea: Revive the substrate deep-trench capacitor of the IBM/New York eDRAM lineage for standalone DRAM: trenches etched ~10 um into silicon beneath the transistor hold ~20 fF, freeing the surface for an 8F2 cell built on existing U.S. logic-fab trench tooling.
why: Escapes the stacked-capacitor AR wall (Fact 1) with charge to spare, allowing 4x longer retention (Fact 3) and no high-AR stack module, at some density cost.

title: Hard-drive flying heads become plasmonic lithography writers
idea: Borrow from storage at rack scale: a Minnesota-made HDD slider carrying a plasmonic ridge aperture flies ~10 nm above a spinning resist-coated wafer at ~10 m/s and writes ~20 nm features with near-field light; 100+ heads write the periodic array as concentric tracks.
why: Maskless sub-20 nm patterning from an all-domestic HDD supply chain at ~1% of EUV tool cost (Fact 4).

title: One accelerator, many printers: shared U.S. free-electron-laser EUV
idea: Jump the light source from tool scale to building scale: one U.S.-built energy-recovery free-electron laser (national-lab heritage) feeds multi-kW EUV through beamlines to 10-20 simple exposure stations that print only the periodic array by reflective interference, avoiding imported projection optics.
why: EUV power per station up 5-10x at lower $/W and breaks the single-supplier scanner chokepoint for array layers.

title: Lattice stepper: a single-pattern projection tool built domestically
idea: Because array layers are one repeating motif, build a stripped-down U.S. DUV projection tool with a permanently mounted mask, no reticle exchange and relaxed stitching, exposing only that motif while periphery runs elsewhere.
why: Tool cost ~$10-20M vs $70-200M, and simple enough for a domestic optics base (fused silica, lens grinding, U.S. excimer lasers).

title: Two-faced wafers: DRAM arrays on front and back
idea: After front-side DRAM is complete, bond to a carrier, thin from the back to ~5 um and build a second array on the backside with U.S. backside-power processing know-how, sharing one periphery through nano-TSVs.
why: ~1.8x bits per crystal pulled and per substrate; the 49% periphery (Fact 7) is amortized over two arrays.

title: Arizona panel-level fan-out replaces TSV stacks for HBM bandwidth
idea: Scale from wafer to 600 mm panels: thin DRAM dies are placed face-down side by side on panels with ~1.5 um-line RDL made on domestic 1X panel steppers, routing ultra-wide buses laterally to the accelerator instead of through TSV stacks.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (Fact 6: 3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss); square panels use ~90% of area vs ~60% for round wafers.

title: Rent idle U.S. logic back-end lines for monolithic memory layers
idea: Turn spare back-end-of-line capacity at U.S. logic fabs into memory capacity: after the logic interconnect, add 6-10 oxide-semiconductor gain-cell layers at <400 C using existing BEOL tools and ArF litho, so memory rides on logic wafers already in production.
why: Near-zero new capex adds supply without a DRAM fab; memory directly above compute cuts data movement (Fact 5).

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM: minutes of retention shrink the capacitor tenfold
idea: Time-shift retention via temperature: at 77 K leakage drops by orders of magnitude, so retention grows from ms to minutes; design the cell around a ~0.5 fF capacitor, delete the high-AR capacitor module, and deploy in U.S. datacenters cooled with domestic LN2 (no helium).
why: Removes the most expensive capacitor steps (Facts 1, 4) and nearly all refresh energy (Fact 3); cooling overhead is absorbed at rack scale.

title: Universal wafer: one mask set, late personalization for every SKU
idea: Run a single DRAM wafer design in U.S. fabs for every product and personalize at the end (I/O width, speed bin, ECC mode, density) through e-fuses, top-metal options and packaging, so the line never changes over.
why: Fewer mask sets (~$20M each), no changeover loss, higher tool utilization and faster yield learning on long single-SKU runs.

title: Strategic DRAM Reserve buys gluts and sells shortages
idea: Time-shift demand risk: a federal reserve buys U.S.-made DRAM wafers at a floor price in gluts and releases them in shortages, like the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, storing unpackaged wafers for years in nitrogen vaults.
why: Damps the boom-bust cycle that makes DRAM capital expensive; a lower risk premium could cut the cost of capital several points.

title: Regulated-utility fab shells depreciated over thirty years
idea: Split the fab's timescales: buildings, utilities and UPW plants (~40% of capex) become a regulated-utility asset with 30-year recovery and a capped return, leasing space to U.S. DRAM makers whose tools stay on short cycles.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (Fact 4); stretching the slow-aging 40% cuts wafer cost ~10-15% and lowers entry capital.

title: Floating nanosphere monolayers mask capacitor holes without scanners
idea: Scale shift to colloids: U.S.-synthesized 25-30 nm silica nanospheres self-pack as a hexagonal monolayer on a Langmuir trough, transfer onto the wafer, are trimmed by plasma, and serve as the etch or lift-off mask for the capacitor lattice.
why: Removes the scanner from the capacitor layer; trough equipment is cheap and domestic.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching digs 200:1 capacitor holes in a bath
idea: Replace plasma etch with catalytic wet etch: a patterned Pt mesh sinks into a sacrificial silicon mold in HF/H2O2 over minutes, carving vertical holes >200:1 that are then lined with capacitor films and the mold removed with the catalyst.
why: Breaks the AR wall (Fact 1) with a wet bench costing ~1% of a high-AR etcher; domestic chemicals and tooling.

title: A million zone plates steered by Texas micromirrors write maskless
idea: Zone-plate array lithography: a plate of ~10^6 diffractive micro-lenses, each switched by a U.S.-made DLP micromirror, focuses its own spot so the whole field is written in parallel without a mask or projection lens.
why: Maskless domestic patterning at ~30-40 nm with a ~$10M tool; pitch splitting finishes the array.

title: Bioreactor-grown protein crystals as nanoscale etch masks
idea: Jump from fermentation tank to wafer: bacterial S-layer proteins grown in U.S. biomanufacturing plants recrystallize on the wafer as 2D lattices with 10-25 nm periodicity, and metal infiltration hardens them into a mask for the capacitor or contact lattice.
why: A litho-free 10-25 nm periodic template at ag-biotech cost (cents per wafer) removes EUV from 1-2 array layers.
